_readme: Start Here listening paths. build.py turns this into site/start.html and site/start/<slug>.html. Edit freely: add/remove/reorder episodes, rewrite the 'why' lines. Episode keys are slugs (ep-043) matching the feed. Keep each path to 4-6 episodes, in the order a new listener should hear them. No em-dashes.

first_three.title: If you only listen to three
first_three.blurb: Three conversations that explain what this show is and why the people on it say things they would not say on a panel.

episodes.why: A senior super on why the jobsite itself is the product nobody designed. The show's thesis in one episode.
Why the biggest GCs are really in the cash business, and what that does to innovation budgets.
The best tool rarely wins the adoption fight. What does, from someone who runs those fights.

paths.title: Running the Job
paths.who: Superintendents, PMs, and PEs managing the daily chaos
paths.blurb: The lessons supers and PMs usually pay for in schedule, money, or sleep. Communication, documentation, scheduling, and the tech that survives contact with a real jobsite.

episodes.why: Wes Juergen on breaking the micromanagement habit when you go from one job to several, and why the field's daily experience is the thing to fix first.
Libby Magliolo on how site leaders lose the room in 90 seconds and the lead-with-the-answer habit that keeps it.
Garrett Mott walks through how one email cost $30 million, and the documentation habits that keep frontline teams out of the deposition chair.
Franco on why most schedules fail and what has to change in how teams build and maintain them.
Chris Massey, Senior Superintendent at EllisDon, on what tech adoption looks like from the trailer rather than the boardroom.
Wally Castro, the super who came up through architecture, on translating between the design side and the field.

paths.title: From the Field to the Corner Office
paths.who: Anyone planning the next ten years of a construction career
paths.blurb: Nobody hands you the playbook for getting from PE to VP. These guests figured it out the hard way: mentorship, visibility, the skills nobody budgets for, and the toll it takes if you ignore the rest of your life.

episodes.why: Sean Johnson's career cheat code: the hospitality and customer-intimacy moves field leaders are never taught but get promoted for.
Mitch McDonald, General Superintendent at XL, on third-generation lessons in leadership and future-proofing a field career.
Chris and Tim Smith on mentorship and coaching, and why the industry's knowledge transfer is mostly informal and mostly broken.
Mark Fly on a career built by saying yes to the strange opportunity, and what the retirement wave means for whoever is next.
Angelo Suntres on the human side of the workforce crisis and the knowledge gap the industry has to close.
Chris Wilocki on navigating a construction career without losing your mental health along the way.

paths.title: Where the GC Business Is Going
paths.who: Owners, executives, and anyone responsible for a P&L
paths.blurb: Margin pressure, the CM fee, owners who grade their contractors, and why the biggest firms struggle to innovate. The conversations about the business of building, not the building.

episodes.why: Aaron Anderson on why big GCs are in the cash business, and how that shapes every innovation decision.
Victor Muchiri on why the CM-fee model is about to break and what could replace it.
Steve Little, an owner who graded his last six GCs. Most of them failed. Hear what he was grading.
Hammad Chaudhry on rethinking the GC model from the partnerships side.
Fouad Khalil on where he would put a billion dollars to fix construction, and why the answer is not technology.
Scott and Chris Massey, a small GC and a big GC, on the AI reset and why you cannot buy your way out.

paths.title: AI Without the Easy Button
paths.who: Anyone being told AI will change their job and wanting to know how
paths.blurb: What AI actually does on a project today, what it does not, and what a contractor should do first. Practitioners and builders, no demos.

episodes.why: Hugh Seaton on why your data does not need to be perfect, and how a contractor should actually start.
Hugh Seaton's first visit: the easy button is a lie, and here is what AI really does for construction.
Tyler Campbell on what project teams are getting wrong about AI, and his doula analogy for helping them through it.
Dr. Sarah Buchner, CEO of Trunk Tools, on what young PMs must know to survive the next five years.
Aaron Toppston on whether white-collar construction work is safe from AI. Asking for a friend.
Patrick Murphy and Jeremy Crumley on what actually matters in preconstruction in the age of AI.

paths.title: Getting the Field to Actually Use It
paths.who: Innovation, VDC, and ops leaders who own rollouts
paths.blurb: Leadership bought it. The field ignores it. Every guest here has lived the gap between a signed contract and a tool people actually open, and most of them have a fix.

episodes.why: Elliot Christiansen on pilots, leadership, and why the best tech rarely wins.
Aaron at Granite on layering tech into the business, citizen development, and when a point solution is dead weight.
Karl Sorensen, Director of Innovation at Davis, on what is and is not working about innovation in construction.
Hannu Lindberg on DPR's foundation for innovation and leading without titles.
Alex Belkofer on how a field-first approach made BIM McCarthy's digital backbone.
Jackie Guilbault on why adoption starts with a story the field believes.

paths.title: Building for the Jobsite
paths.who: Contech founders, product, and go-to-market teams
paths.blurb: What practitioners actually think of your product, how GCs really buy, and why the org chart on the other side of the table matters more than your roadmap.

episodes.why: Charles Ma on bootstrapping a construction SaaS company and why the customer's org chart is killing innovation.
Cameron Page on the hard truth about going from the jobsite to founding ClearStory.
KP Reddy on why a contech VC stopped investing in SaaS.
Aaron Toppston on the VC playbook for construction innovation.
Michael Zeppieri on the brutal truth about construction tech nobody wants to admit.
Al Ricci's masterclass on three decades of selling and servicing construction technology.

paths.title: The Talent Cliff
paths.who: Leaders watching the experience walk out the door
paths.blurb: The boomers are retiring, the knowledge is not written down, and the next generation learns differently. What the industry is doing about it, and what it is not.

episodes.why: Steve Dell'Orto on digitizing your brain before you retire, and the talent cliff coming for precon.
Mark Fly on the retirement wave and why the industry cannot afford to lose any more boomers.
Angelo Suntres on the knowledge gap at the center of the workforce crisis.
Matt Graves, the Construction Yeti, on why training the next generation means building better content.
Chris and Tim Smith on mentorship as the industry's actual knowledge-transfer system.
